📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is almost here, and it reminds us that a good open world needs more than a lot of buildings. It needs places that feel as though they existed before you arrived and will carry on after you've driven off. In GTA 6, Rockstar is trying to achieve that by thinking about the people behind every home, business and building in Leonida.

According to recent reports, “For every visual design, we are getting into the heads of the people who would have inhabited that place and role-playing how the final look would have come about,” says Miriam Bellard, Vice President of Art: Visual Development. “Would they have hired an architect or DIY’d it? Are they trying to express their status and prestige, or is it all about comfort and practicalities? Are they messy or tidy? What is their taste?”.

In a recent development, it's a wonderfully practical way to approach world-building, and after playing GTA 6 for three weeks, I can say each building feels unique yet makes sense, both to explore and to use within the game's world. Rather than designing a building as an isolated piece of architecture, the team imagines the decisions behind it. That gives each place a personality, whether it's somewhere industrial, scruffy, decadent or dangerous.

“I love that we get to do that for such a wide variety of people and places,” Bellard adds. “Everything from industrial to scruffy to decadent to dangerous. We get to design all of that – and it’s lots of fun!”.

It has been revealed that that variety matters in a world inspired by Florida, where the landscape shifts between sun-soaked beaches, retirement communities, rural enclaves, and high-end shopping districts. John Macpherson, Senior Design Director: World & Population, notes reference trips and time spent with locals helped the team capture the state's “raw energy and vibrant chaos”.

According to recent reports, the result is a world where even a building's appearance can tell you something about who lives or works there, and I found it can also help you blueprint heists and robberies by understanding the flow of a bank or store. Moreover, Rockstar's designers and artists have played with Vice City and the State's history, building wear and tear and architectural trends into its world. In GTA 6, architecture is another way to get to know Leonida.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The auction houses’ marquee evening sales get all the headlines, with high-eight-figure artworks and high-nine-figure totals, sometimes approaching the billion-dollar mark when the market is flush.

Recent findings suggest that but the more modest daytime sales of lower-priced materials occasionally contain real treasures. When I wrote about them for Artnet News in 2015, experts told me that this is where the houses make a lot of their profits; dealers haunt these sales to stock up on inventory; they are far less stage-managed than the evening events; they may be more indicative of the actual health of the market; and you can find better deals. Related Articles Christie's Buzzy 20th-Century Sale Totals $626.6 M., with Starry Lots Above $80 M. by Kandinsky and Klimt Seven Works Reportedly from Jeff Koons's Collection Fetch a Lackluster $104 M. at Christie's, Led by a $31.2 M. Picasso.

And they can occasionally spark serious bidding wars. On Wednesday, a tiny artwork by a titan of French Impressionism became the latest example.

According to recent reports, claude Monet’s La Barque (ca. 1874), which came under the hammer at Christie’s Rockefeller Center saleroom at a day sale of Impressionist and modern art, was estimated at $300,000 to $500,000, but fetched just shy of $7 million. Its modest estimate matched its diminutive size: it measures only 2¾ by 3½ inches, so it sold for $722,285.71 per square inch.

More than 20 bidders fought for the tiny panel, some in the room and some bidding on the phone via Christie’s specialists, says the house; the contest went on for six minutes and 45 seconds, and Rachel White Young, head of the 20th-century evening sale, won the prize for her client.

Even before making a little auction history on Wednesday, the painting had an unusual backstory.

Sources indicate that paris art dealer Georges Petit, a collector and supporter of the Impressionists, commissioned it from the artist; the magazine L’Art Moderne wrote about it in June 1902, relating how the collector carried around small pieces of wood, cut to identical sizes, which he handed out to artists he admired. He would offer them 100 francs and ask if they would return the petite panel as a painting. He did the same with Camille Corot, Édouard Manet, Camille Pissarro, and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, all of whom obliged.

All five would come into the collection of Thérèse and Frédéric Humbert, notorious figures in French high society. She claimed to have been willed a fortune by an imaginary American millionaire, Robert Crawford, whose life she had supposedly saved. They borrowed against an imaginary fortune, buying a grand home and occupying the center of Parisian social life for two decades, until bank officials started asking questions and her creditors sued and the tissue of lies was shredded.

In a recent development, funny enough, the resulting sale of their possessions would take place in 1902 at none other than Galerie Georges Petit. Galerie Bernheim-Jeune bought it and it remained with that family until 2013, when the ollectors Marlene and Spencer Hays got it at Paris auction house Hôtel Drouot, for the hammer price of €200,000. They began selling books door-to-door as a summer job for Southwestern Manufacturer and later went on to run the busines and start a clothing company.

According to their foundation, when asked what was the most fun part of their lives, they would say, “learning about art and building a collection that we treasure,” but would also quote Sir Richard Attenborough to the effect that art collectors are “simply its temporary, fortunate and delighted custodians.” Their collection included works by Pierre Bonnard, Edgar Degas, Henri Matisse, Amedeo Modigliani, and Édouard Vuillard.

They were as good as their word; they granted their collection to Paris’s Musée d’Orsay in 2016. It was the largest foreign collection donated since World War II, with some 600 masterworks from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He died the next year, survived by Marlene.

According to recent reports, this redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating**, and it's worth being specific about where the friction lives — because once you understand it, most of the difficulty evaporates. **The earning is easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards points flow into World of Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, and Chase is one of the most accessible premium rewards ecosystems for newly introduced-to-intermediate travel rewards participants. The points pipeline is well-established and reliable. **The transfer and booking mechanics are easy.** The actual process — confirm availability, transfer points, complete booking — is straightforward if you follow the correct sequence. The Hyatt website is functional and the award search is transparent. **The hard part is availability.** Park Hyatt properties are genuinely popular, the award inventory is limited, and the most desirable dates (cherry blossom season, major holidays, Fashion Week) book out fast. This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Initiative further ahead than feels natural. If you want Tokyo in April of next year, you should be searching in late March or early April of the current year. 2. **Be flexible by 3–5 days on either side.** Award inventory often opens mid-week when demand is lower. Shifting from a Saturday check-in to a Thursday can unlock availability that doesn't exist on peak nights. 3. **Check repeatedly near the 30-day mark.** Properties occasionally release additional award space as the date approaches. Setting a weekly reminder to re-check your target dates costs nothing. If you're willing to plan ahead and stay flexible on exact dates, moderate difficulty becomes very manageable — and the reward on the other side is worth every bit of the effort.

#45503. Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year revealed

Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year revealed

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London.
  • The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico.
  • Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London.

The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico.

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.

Leisure and wellness projects win significant again.

The judges hailed the biophilic project as “beautifully minimalist with a spiritual touch of the soul”.

“It’s totally fresh, totally innovative, and never seen before,” they added.

The win marks the second consecutive year that the leisure and wellness project of the year has gone on to claim the overall sector title, following Herzog & de Meuron’s win last year.

Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi.

The winning project of the year was up against category winners including a sprawling brick-clad university building modelled on stepped wells in India, a country house with walls formed of unstabilised rammed earth in the UK and a project featuring an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through in Mexico.

A housing project that appears as if emerging from the natural landscape and a viewpoint designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the burial site of a legendary Viking were also amongst the category winners.

Read more about all the winning architecture projects below:.

Architecture project of the year and leisure and wellness project of the year: Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi.

The project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.

Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly.

The idea for the project was to make the trees feel part of the architecture, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

“Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly,” stated the master jury.

“It is a building that offers a spiritual connection between humans and nature.”.

House (urban) project of the year: Amami House by Sakai Architects.

Local studio Sakai Architects won urban house of the year for its off-grid home on Amami Ōshima, an island in the Amami archipelago off Japan‘s southern coast.

This house reveals how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature.

The design was informed by the region’s traditional materials and crafts and its development was spurred by the increase in extreme weather conditions on the island.

“This house reveals how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature,” the master jury mentioned.

“In a time of climate crisis, it offers an excellent solution for autonomy of energy, while smartly reinterpreting the arrangement and materials of a traditional Japanese house.”.

House (rural) project of the year: Jiang Deng Lu by Shisuo Design Office.

Shisuo Design Office won rural house of the year for Jiang Deng Lu in Anhui, China.

This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result.

The compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site and made using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

“This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result,” stated the judges.

“Innovative in its use of available materials, the project is highly resolved, with incredible quality of light and generosity of space despite a small footprint.”.

Housing project of the year: La Querola by Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos.

Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos won housing project of the year for La Querola in Ordino, Andorra.

A deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core.

Made up of seven irregularly shaped blocks embedded into the sloping valley and clad in locally sourced slate, the building’s facades feature recessed windows and openings revealing outdoor terraces.

The judges commended the development’s trend-bucking design as a “deliberately expressionist project, celebrating forms that are not repeatable”.

Sources indicate that “It’s a deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core. It’s unconventional, unique, controversial, and a very strong statement,” they noted.

Recently, a fire damaged all seven buildings in the uninhabited development. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

House renovation of the year: Haniyasu House by Aatismo.

Local architecture studio Aatismo won house renovation of the year for Haniyasu House, a home in the coastal town of Kamakura, Japan.

It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability.

The project saw the single-storey home, originally built in 1967, stripped back to its timber frame after a typhoon had left it structurally unsound, and boldly characterised with rough walls streaked with clay, soil and metal powders to evoke ceramic glazes.

The judges praised the project’s sensitivity to “the history of both the architecture and its owners”.

“It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability,” they added.

House extension of the year: Golmorad by ZAV Architects.

Iranian studio ZAV Architects won house extension of the year for its project featuring a series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue in Tehran, Iran.

It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life.

Transforming the residence from a weekend villa into a permanent home, its arched series of overlapping arched roofs appears as if organically growing from the home.

The judges found the extension to be “playful with a sense of freedom,” adding that, “it doesn’t manipulate the old house in any way, but instead seems to organically extend it in a very unpredictable direction.”.

“It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life,” they remarked.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Civic project of the year: Zando Central Market by Think Tank Architecture.

French studio Think Tank Architecture won civic project of the year for its geometric brick-and-concrete market in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo.

A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves.

The newly introduced building, with space for 20,000 vendors, replaces a historic market on the same site in the capital that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

“A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves, and a capacity to serve the community in a really large-scale way,” said the master jury.

“It has a variety within it to allow a lot of activity to take place, with materials that are simple but sustainable.”.

Cultural project of the year: Ismaili Center Houston by Farshid Moussavi Architecture.

Farshid Moussavi Architects won cultural project of the year for its Ismaili Center in Houston, United States.

A very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner.

The building and its sprawling gardens is the first Ismaili Center in the US and is one of several around the world commissioned by the current Imam, or spiritual leader, of the Shia Ismaili Muslim community to serve as a place of worship and cultural exchange.

The judges praised it as a “very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner”.

“It has a stunning relationship to light, and incredible detailing and materiality,” they added.

Workplace project (small) of the year: Carpenter’s Home by Primary Architects.

Chinese studio Primary Architects won small workplace project of the year for its undulating timber roof-topped studio in Xinyang, China.

The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities.

The project, a local carpenter’s studio, was designed by the practice to incorporate the craftsman’s studio, as well as a woodcraft workshop that is also open to the public.

“A beautiful project that goes above and beyond the brief,” commended the judges.

“The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities.”.

Workplace project (large) of the year: Florentia Village by Turner Works.

Architecture studio Turner Works won large workplace project of the year for Florentia Village, London.

Well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour.

The practice transformed an old textile manufacturing site in London’s Harringay Warehouse District into a creative hub that offers flexible workshops, studios and industrial units ranging from 46 to 1,400 square metres, alongside community spaces and a cafe.

The judges praised it as “well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour,” as well as the buildings being “highly flexible, with spaces designed to reinforce a sense of community”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Education project of the year: Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects.

Sanjay Puri Architects won education project of the year for its sprawling brick-clad university building in Indore, India.

In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most new constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould.

Referencing traditional stepped wells found in the country, its defining feature is its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof, which comprises 463 stepped platforms that can be used as individual social spaces or as a singular auditorium for up to 9,000 people.

“This project creates its own universe,” said the master jury.

“In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most newly introduced constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould,” they continued.

“The massing of the roof reduces scale and creates interesting courtyards, creating spaces that feel appropriate for both the place and its climate.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Heritage project of the year: Olympics Utilities by Chartier-Corbasson Architects.

French studio Chartier-Corbasson Architectes won heritage project of the year for its transformation of a neglected underground passage beneath Paris, France.

It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant.

Located in a passage beneath the Trocadero Gardens, the studio created a public restroom, using an industrial-feeling palette of stainless and weathered steel to highlight its thoughtful, utilitarian design while giving it a newly introduced purpose.

“It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant,” remarked the judges.

“The project creates architectural character, while also preserving a connection to 19th-century futuristic architecture. Unusual, but iconic.”.

Hospitality project of the year: Perma by Mold Architects.

Perma by Mold Architects in Serifos, Greece won hospitality project of the year, sponsored by Sanderson.

There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint.

Comprising five guest houses, the rugged retreat on the island of Serifos was constructed by using material extracted during construction to build much of the retreat itself, rather than removing the hillside and building on top of it.

The judges praised its “striking architecture”, noting it as “very innovative in its programmatic possibilities”.

“There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint,” they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Infrastructure and transport project of the year: Naples Underground Central Station by Miralles Tagliabue EMBT.

Spanish architecture studio EMBT won infrastructure and transport project of the year for Naples Underground Central Station in Italy.

A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train.

Contrasting its modernist surroundings with a wavy timber roof, the 10,000-square-metre building was designed to replace a previously understated metro entrance with a latest public plaza that felt more integrated with the surrounding city.

The judges commended the project as a “successful urban space, both elegant and spatially interesting.”.

According to recent reports, “A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train,” they continued. “The use of timber is also impressive.”.

Small project of the year: Ring of Bjólfur by Arkibygg Architects.

Local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture won small project of the year for their mountain viewpoint in Seyðisfjörður, Iceland.

A minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way.

Designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.

The master jury hailed the viewpoint as a “minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way,” adding that, “the minimal use of material maximises the experience”.

Mixed-use project of the year: York Minster Centre of Excellence by Tonkin Liu.

Architecture studio Tonkin Liu won mixed-use project of the year for its two timber buildings on either side of a Grade I-listed Gothic cathedral in York, United Kingdom.

The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a latest generation of makers using the space.

Named The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills, the buildings include the rectangular Heritage Quad and the triangular Technology Hub, both of which give working stonemasons views of the historic York Minster cathedral.

“There is a real honesty in the combination of buildings, with a unique roofing structure,” noted the judges.

“The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a new generation of makers using the space,” they added.

Landscape and urban design of the year: Parque del Jaguar by Colectivo C733.

Mexican studio Colectivo C733 won landscape and urban design of the year for its work across Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.

Despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects.

The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s key habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.

It features an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest, as well as a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals’ habitat while allowing people to explore the area.

The judges praised the project as “rooted in its context, made for locals as well as tourists,” adding that, “despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects.”.

Sustainable building of the year: Rammed Earth House by Tuckey Design Studio.

Rammed Earth house by Tuckey Design Studio in Wiltshire, United Kingdom, won sustainable building of the year, sponsored by Michelmersh.

Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe.

Built on the site of a former brickworks, the rural country house was constructed from both the clay underfoot and an aggregate made from crushed demolition waste to form unstabilised rammed earth walls.

As a form of earth construction that is largely untested at such scale in the UK, the judges commended the project as “a radical example of material innovation”.

“Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe,” they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Sustainable renovation of the year: De Nederlandsche Bank by Mecanoo.

Dutch firm Mecanoo won sustainable renovation of the year for its major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank in Amsterdam.

An admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building.

The project involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault, seeing a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.

The renovation was praised as “an admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building,” by the master jury, who also noted its efforts to adapt it to a different use “while also addressing material and energy concerns.”.

According to recent reports, dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology tech giant Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

#45502. Led by Record-Breaking $190.4 M. van Gogh, Sotheby’s Impressionist and Modern Art Sales Rake in $777.8 M.

Led by Record-Breaking $190.4 M. van Gogh, Sotheby’s Impressionist and Modern Art Sales Rake in $777.8 M.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1406 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was an evening of superlatives at Sotheby’s, whose two auctions of Impressionist and modern art in New York tonight brought in a total of $777.8 million.
  • That total is the highest one for a single night at the auction house, edging past the $706 million achieved last November at the house’s inaugural evening double-header at the Breuer building.
  • Two lots in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection were the most anticipated paintings of the season: Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890) and Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888–90).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was an evening of superlatives at Sotheby’s, whose two auctions of Impressionist and modern art in New York tonight brought in a total of $777.8 million.

That total is the highest one for a single night at the auction house, edging past the $706 million achieved last November at the house’s inaugural evening double-header at the Breuer building. And while the 12 lots from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection came in at $412 million, just shy of their presale low estimate of $414.5 million, those dozen works still managed to set a record for a single-owner evening sale dedicated to Impressionist and modern art at Sotheby’s. (Unless otherwise noted, prices cited here are inclusive of fees.) Related Articles Cézanne 'Arlequin' Sells for $111 M. at Sotheby's, Becoming One of the Most Expensive Paintings by the Artist Van Gogh Slashes Auction Record at Sotheby's, Selling for $190.4 M.

Two lots in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection were the most anticipated paintings of the season: Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890) and Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888–90).

Sources indicate that they both achieved eye-popping prices—$190.4 million for the van Gogh, the artist’s highest price to date and the highest price for any work of art ever sold at Sotheby’s, and $111 million for the Cézanne, the second-highest price for Cézanne at auction. But the bidding was anticlimactic.

Sources indicate that both works hammered below their pre-sale estimates. There was just a smattering of bids on the van Gogh. The Cézanne inched along with four bids alternating between Sotheby’s specialists Lisa Dennison, Chairman Americas, and Helena Newman, chairman of Sotheby’s Europe. It hammered to Newman.

Asked after the sale whether the publicity surrounding the restitution claim against the van Gogh had affected bidding, Sotheby’s CEO Charles Stewart stated he didn’t think so.

“First of all, it’s a record price for the artist,” he said, pointing out that it was also the fourth-highest price achieved by any artist at auction. “I think you have to separate auction heat from auction results,” he said.

Sources indicate that the liveliest bidding came for the final two paintings, both of them with estimates on the lower side, for this sale. Edith Eustis and Simon Stark on the phones, as well as several bidders in the room, went for Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec’s Femme assise de profil vers la gauche (1890). It sold to a man in the second row for $3.8 million. Then, Wendy Lin, Serena Hildebrandt, and Alina Davey battled on the phones for the Camille Pissarro landscape, Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875). It came down to Lin and Davey, and went to Davey for $2 million. It was bought by the same bidder who bought Edgar Degas’s Avant la course (ca. 1893) for $18 million a few lots earlier, bidding with Sotheby’s Ben Doller.

Things picked up considerably during the 47-lot, multiple-owner sale that followed, which saw lively bidding in the room and no fewer than 33 Sotheby’s specialists fielding bids over the phones. All told, this sale made $365.8 million, with all but one of the lots sold. It helped that the highest-priced lots came early in the sale and generated heated bidding wars.

According to recent reports, the top price from that sale was the $47.3 million for Edward Hopper’s 1944 seascape The Martha Mckeen of Wellfleet, from the collection of Baroness Carmen Thyssen-Bornemisza. It’s far from Hopper’s record—$91.8 million for Chop Suey from the Barney Ebsworth collection at Christie’s in November 2018—but it is his second-highest price at auction. As dealer Lock Kresler pointed out on the Nota Bene podcast, the closest comparison is another Hopper seascape, Blackwell’s Island, from 1928, which sold at Christie’s in 2013 for $19.1 million.

The Martha Mckeen sparked a bidding war between four Sotheby’s specialists on the phone bank, with Scott Niichel, vice chairman and head of middle market for modern and contemporary art, coming out the winner. Accounting for fees, the work made $47.8 million.

It has been revealed that close behind the Hopper was the $45 million achieved by Rene Magritte’s 1964 painting L’Ami de l’ordre, which stars the painter’s famous man in a bowler hat. It came from the collection of Sydell Miller, who bought it in 1998 for a mere $5.3 million. The previous record for a bowler hat painting was for the one sold at Christie’s London in March 2024 for £33.7 million (about $43.2 million), Magritte’s third-highest price. Several bidders in the room went up against two Sotheby’s specialists, Jackie Wachter and Bame Fierro March. A bidder in the room was the winner, but no one seemed to be able to identify him.

It has been revealed that also adding sparks early in the sale was Aaron Douglas’s 1931 painting of Harriet Tubman. Even if it had merely sold near its pre-sale estimate of $2.5 million–$3.5 million, the piece would have handily broken the record for Douglas: $600,000, for a piece sold at Swann Galleries auction house in 2008. But it more than quadrupled that estimate to make $14.1 million, all of which will go to Bennett College, a historically Black women’s college, that sold the piece.

In a recent development, some eight bidders went after the painting, beginning with Jackie Wachter going up against her father, George Wachter, who serves as Sotheby’s chairman of North America and South America. Several bidders in the room popped in before Sotheby’s head of American art Stefany Morris entered the war. In the end, it was Morris versus the room, with Morris the winner.

“We knew it was going to make a massive price,” Sotheby’s vice chairman and head of contemporary art David Galperin said after the sale. “That’s one of the most exciting auction moments—when you have something that is so categorically the very best” by an artist whose work rarely comes to auction.

Recent findings suggest that halfway through the sale came another massive moment: a painting by Mary Cassatt, Summertime (1894–95), from the Armand Hammer collection, sold for $13.3 million, a new record that nearly doubles the previous one, $7.5 million. Here the evening’s depth of bidding was again on display: specialists David Galperin, Caroline Seabolt, Lin, and Simon Stock all went after it, but the winner was an online bidder.

Industry observers note that on the lower end of the price spectrum, a landscape by Chaim Soutine, Place à Céret (1921–22), estimated at just $800,000–$1.2 million, made $3.9 million. Five Sotheby’s specialists on the phones wanted the picture; so did bidders in the room. Jen Hua, deputy chairman of Sotheby’s Asia, cast the final bid.

Over the course of the evening, Hua and Lin, the Sotheby’s Asia chairman, were especially busy. Asian collectors bought works by Signac, Maurice de Vlaminck, Cézanne, Claude Monet, Renoir, Soutine, Egon Schiele, and Degas (including the Degas in the Blaquier-Arrieta sale for $18 million). They bid on works by Monet (the Blaquier-Arrieta picture that sold for $20.2 million), Picasso, Magritte, Cassatt, and Degas.

The sale was not without hitches. A Remedios Varo drawing failed to sell, and three lots—pieces by Magritte, Cézanne, and Matisse—were apparently withdrawn while the sale was in progress, given that the withdrawals were not declared prior to the sale, as is customary. (Two of the withdrawn lots–Henri Matisse’s La Jetée à Collioure (estimate $5–$7 million), and Paul Cézanne’s L’Oncle Dominique (estimate $3–$5 million)–are among the 11 in the sale that come from the collection of George Weiss, the hedge fund founder now in bankruptcy, as ARTnews revealed earlier this month.).

Every one of the Blaquier lots was guaranteed. For Phillip Hoffman, founder and chairman of the Fine Art Group, that brought up a question about Sotheby’s strategy.

Industry observers note that “The guarantees were just too high,” he told ARTnews immediately after the Blaquier-Arrieta sale. “I think these guarantees are just pushing the limit.”.

He remarked Sotheby’s had left buyers very little room to compete, and had been too confident in its pricing, with the result a string of lots that attracted little meaningful competition.

Calling it “a little bit of overconfidence” on the house’s part, he speculated that they might have lost as much as $50 million on guarantees.

Stewart, the Sotheby’s CEO, defended the house’s approach to the evening.

Sources indicate that “Our estimates weren’t shy,” he acknowledged. “You can read into that whatever you like. We were happy with the result of everything.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dezeen has announced the six winners of Dezeen Awards 2026 Designers of the Year at this evening’s ceremony in London, which include Lina Ghotmeh, Keiji Ashizawa and Yinka Ilori.

Our Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.

This year, Ghotmeh took home the architect of the year award, while studio duo Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo were named emerging architect of the year.

Interior designer of the year was awarded to Tokyo-based Ashizawa, and Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was named emerging interior designer of the year.

London-based Ilori won designer of the year with Stockholm-based Simon Skinner named emerging designer of the year.

Read more about the Designers of the Year below:.

Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet.

Architect of the year: Lina Ghotmeh.

It has been revealed that ghotmeh, who is the founder of architecture practice Lina Ghotmeh Architecture, is one of the world’s most sought-after architects. Among her high-profile projects was the 2023 Serpentine Pavilion and she was recently appointed to renovate the British Museum’s Western Range galleries.

“From Beirut to Paris and beyond, Lina Ghotmeh creates architecture that feels both rooted in history and entirely of the future,” mentioned the judges.

According to recent reports, “Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet. We anticipate her studio continuing to go from strength to strength.”.

Recent findings suggest that ghotmeh is known for her sustainable and historically rooted designs, including the Stone Garden apartment block in Beruit, which was named architecture project of the year at Dezeen Awards 2021. She has received multiple accolades, including being named on the Time100 Next list in 2025 and winning the 2023 Great Arab Minds Award.

Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.

Emerging architect of the year: Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo.

Founded by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect and urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa is an emerging architecture studio with offices in France, Spain and Japan.

“Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo’s emerging practice brings a fresh sense of curiosity to architecture, balancing bold forms and material experimentation with tactility and unexpected gestures,” mentioned the judges.

“Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.”.

Among the studio’s varied and intriguing work is Nakano House in Japan’s Fukuoka prefecture – an apartment block informed by the design of a traditional Japanese engawa.

His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.

Interior designer of the year: Keiji Ashizawa.

Interior designer Ashizawa runs his interdisciplinary, craft-oriented studio based on the ideal of “honest design”. Along with interior spaces, his Tokyo-based studio designs everything from lighting to furniture and products.

“Prolific designer Keiji Ashizawa brings a quiet confidence to interior design, where natural materials, considered details, refined craftsmanship and a sense of calm take centre stage,” stated the judges.

“His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.”.

Recent work from the studio includes a tea shop in central Shanghai, a holiday home clad in charred cedar in central Japan and a showroom for Japanese furniture brand Karimoku.

Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.

Emerging interior designer of the year: Yasmine Ghoniem.

Australian designer Ghoniem has found great success since founding her interior studio YSG in 2020 with the aim of creating bold, holistic design experiences.

“Yasmine Ghoniem takes a bold, instinctive approach to interior design, bringing together rich textures, unexpected colour and cultural references,” mentioned the judges.

“Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.”.

Among her recent – and varied – designs are a wellness hotel in Bali, the revamp of a Sydney apartment, a warehouse conversion in Sydney designed to evoke the Mojave desert and a bar for gin brand Four Pillars.

Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.

Designer of the year: Yinka Ilori.

Ilori designs pavilions, installations, pop-ups, products and furniture, all united by a bold use of colour informed by his Nigerian heritage.

“Yinka Ilori injects design with an irresistible dose of colour, humour and optimism, turning everyday objects and spaces into lively celebrations of culture and community,” said the judges.

“Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.”.

Recent findings suggest that ilori has designed numerous pavilions, including the Colour Palace in London and an events space for the Estrel Berlin hotel in Germany. On a smaller scale, he has designed products including a watch for Swiss brand MB&F and his own range of branded homeware.

He also recently created an extensive collection of furniture, fabrics and homeware for Dunelm.

Simon Skinner is a burgeoning talent who brings a fresh perspective to contemporary Scandinavian design, pairing a thoughtful approach to materials with a refined, understated visual language.

Emerging designer of the year: Simon Skinner.

Swedish designer Skinner is well-known for his furniture, sculpture and installations that explore how materials can be rethought or reused.

Sources indicate that “Simon Skinner is a burgeoning talent who brings a fresh perspective to contemporary Scandinavian design, pairing a thoughtful approach to materials with a refined, understated visual language. His work subverts the familiar, creating distinct new objects that hint at an exciting new direction for design.”.

Recent examples of his varied, multidisciplinary work include a range of sculptural lights made from second-hand bowls, ashtrays and cat figurines.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

It has been revealed that that’s the running total, inclusive of buyer’s fees, that Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips have sold at the three evening sales held in New York this week. At Sotheby’s on Monday night, a double header sale generated a total of $378.7 million, with the white-glove Baum collection bringing in $110 million and the contemporary sale realized $268.8 million. The top lots, respectively, were Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest (1960) for $19.3 million and Roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990) for $24.7 million. Tuesday evening saw first Phillips sell $104.4 million in art and then Christie’s having a haul of $626.6 million. Amedeo Modigliani’s Tête (1911–12) led the Phillips auction, selling for $44.6 million, while a short bidding war saw Wassily Kandinsky’s Betonte Ecken (1922–23) go for $85.8 million, a new record for the artist. Christie’s set records for four other artists (Wifredo Lam, Cornelius Cornelisz. van Haarlem, Fernando Botero, and Hans Bellmer), while Sotheby’s also saw five records on Monday (for Yayoi Kusama, Sam Francis, Jonas Wood, Firelei Báez, and Tomma Abts.).

Sources indicate that while we’re on the topic of Sotheby’s, Christie’s, and Phillips, the New York Times published this week a feature looking at how Phillips’s recent decision not to compete with the other two houses. Calling Phillips “always an underdog in the auction world,” reporters Zachary Small and Julia Halperin got the house’s chief executive, Martin Wilson, to say, “One client described us as scrappers and I loved that description.” At least to my mind, that doesn’t come off as intended. Though it would seem that Phillips has admitted defeat and retreated like a dog with its tail between its legs, Wilson said that the house no longer believes in growing for the sake of growing, especially at the expense of profitability. It’s been a year of change for Phillips’s top brass, with several executives departing, as ARTnews previously reported. One of them, former Asia chairman Jonathan Crockett, told the Times that his decision to leave was based on the fact that this “strategy no longer resonated with me.”.

For more auction-related coverage, might I suggest reading three pieces from ARTnews regarding controversies over whether or not a work would actually make it to the block. There’s the $180 million Vincent van Gogh painting that will be auctioned by Sotheby’s tonight after a last-minute settlement. Two Gothic paintings are to be sold on Saturday in Germany despite claims to stop the sales. And there’s a Frida Kahlo painting that was pulled from last night’s Christie’s evening sale. But, if I were you, I’d skip Jerry Saltz’s latest, an overly “sentimental” column, bemoaning last night’s sale of works owned by the reportedly cash-strapped artist Jeff Koons. Despite his objections, the works sold for $104 million, or the sale’s low estimate.

Industry News: Cricut Maker 5 review: A smaller, smarter cutting machine for serious crafters

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Cricut Maker 5 isn't a massive leap from the Maker 4, but it's smaller, lighter, easier to set up and can cut materials up to 3mm thick.
  • Rotary blade, knife blade and FabricGrip mat cost extra.
  • In a recent development, why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Cricut Maker 5 isn't a massive leap from the Maker 4, but it's smaller, lighter, easier to set up and can cut materials up to 3mm thick. It also keeps the versatility that makes the Maker range so appealing, from intricate paper designs and vinyl stickers to engraving metal and cutting fabric.

Smaller and lighter than earlier Makers.

Huge range of tools and materials.

Up to twice as fast as the Maker 3.

Little reason for Maker 4 owners to upgrade.

Rotary blade, knife blade and FabricGrip mat cost extra.

In a recent development, why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Price: $349 / £349.99 machine only, $399 / £399.99 Essential Bundle, $529 / £499.99 Ultimate Bundle.

Dimensions: 50.2 x 19.1 x 11.9cm.

Cutting speed: Up to 14.1 inches per second.

Materials support: 300+ compatible materials.

Maximum cutting speed: 3mm (depending on material and tool).

Compatible tools: 13, including engraving.

Maximum Smart Material cut length: 3.6m (12ft).

Maximum cut area: 29.2 x 59.7cm with a large mat.

Connectivity: Bluetooth Low Energy, USB-C.

I've been using Cricut machines for years, mostly for quilting and personalised craft projects, and what keeps me coming back to the Maker range is how much one machine can do. The Maker 5 keeps that going. Cuts are accurate, it's quick, and Design Space makes projects easy to start, whether you work from a template or design your own.

If you own the older Maker 3, I'd seriously consider upgrading: the faster cutting and more compact body are noticeable straight away. If you already have the slightly newer Maker 4, it's a harder argument to make, because Maker 5 tidies up the older machine and makes subtle improvements rather than replacing it, and the Maker 4 is still an excellent cutter.

It has been revealed that for anyone choosing a first Cricut, the Maker 5 is a great option, provided you'll use its extra capabilities. If you mostly make cards, stickers and vinyl decorations, the cheaper Explore range may be all you need.

In this Maker 5 review, I go into detail on what the new craft machine can do, how to use it, and how it compares with recent Cricut releases.

The first thing I noticed was the colour. The Slate Blue finish is a soft grey-blue that looks more contemporary than earlier Makers. It's also a lot smaller, with Cricut claiming a 30% reduction in size compared with earlier machines. At around 50cm wide, 19cm deep and 12cm high, it takes up noticeably less room on my desk, and at 4.9kg it's lighter than the Maker 4, so it's easy to move or put away. That's handy if you have a dedicated craft room, and even more so if, like me, you sometimes have to share your workspace with other projects.

The lid includes a storage tray to keep tools close at hand, and the overall design feels neat and considered.

According to recent reports, setup is straightforward. Head to the Cricut website, select the Maker 5 and follow the instructions. It tells you how much room you need in front of and behind the machine for materials and mats to feed through, and reminds you to remove the packaging before you start. Plug it in, open Design Space on your computer, and follow the prompts. The machine connects over Bluetooth; there's no separate on/off switch to worry about, and the software talks you through loading material and starting each job.

Sources indicate that the Maker 5 comes with a 12 x 12 in LightGrip mat, a cutting tool, a scoring tool, and a dual-sided black marker, plus materials for your first project. Depending on the bundle, you may also get a portable trimmer.

If you're upgrading from an older Cricut, many of your existing tools carry over, including mats, fine-point blades, and many older Maker tools, as well as Smart Materials such as vinyl and iron-on. The new snap-in pen holder has different compatibility requirements, though, so check your pens before assuming they'll fit.

According to recent reports, the rotary blade for cutting fabric and specialist blades such as the knife blade for thicker materials are extra purchases. They matter most if you're buying the Maker for quilting or more ambitious projects.

It has been revealed that the Maker 5 cuts up to 14.1 inches per second, which is fast, but the Maker 4 already offered that speed, so don't expect a dramatic difference if you're upgrading from that model. Maker 3 owners will notice more: like the Maker 4, the Maker 5 cuts up to twice as fast, which really shows when you're working through multiple designs or larger projects.

According to recent reports, it handles more than 300 compatible materials, from delicate paper and vinyl to leather, fabric and selected thicker materials. It can cut, draw, score, engrave and deboss, and it works with a home printer for full-colour Print Then Cut projects.

Smart Materials are a substantial part of the Cricut experience. They feed straight into the machine without a cutting mat, which makes longer designs much easier. Smart Vinyl, for example, can be loaded directly for continuous cuts of up to 12ft. Leftover vinyl doesn't have to go to waste either, as you can stick smaller pieces onto a Cricut mat.

For standard cardstock, vinyl and iron-on projects, the Maker 5 is very easy to use. Design Space tells you which material to select, which blade or tool to load and when to feed the mat into the machine, so you spend more time creating and less time worrying about settings.

Sources indicate that this is where the Maker 5 earns its place as Cricut's flagship. The Explore range handles everyday crafting well, but I'd recommend the Maker to anyone serious about quilting, sewing or fabric projects. In fact, anything that requires more power and precision.

Recent findings suggest that the rotary blade cuts fabric accurately and quickly, without endless measuring or hand-cutting shapes. You'll need to buy the rotary blade and housing separately, along with a pink FabricGrip mat, available in 12 x 12 inches and 12 x 24 inches.

For quilters, that's a huge time-saver. Design Space offers a selection of quilting blocks and templates, with components separated into shapes and colours, ready for cutting. Take the half-square triangle, a quilting staple that's surprisingly fiddly to cut by hand. You're cutting on the bias, so accuracy matters if the pieces are going to line up.

In Design Space, I create a square, add a diagonal line and change the line operation to Cut. After rotating it by 45 degrees, I position it over the square, select both elements and attach them. The result is two accurately cut triangles, ready to use. When you're making a quilt with dozens or even hundreds of identical pieces, having the machine do the repetitive cutting makes a real difference.

The Maker can also handle thicker, more demanding materials than the Explore machines, up to 3mm. Add a knife blade, another extra, and selected wood and chipboard projects open up too.

Recent findings suggest that engraving is one of my favourite things about the Maker 5. I photographed my house, uploaded it to Design Space, and used the software to prepare the image for engraving on an aluminium sheet. I was thrilled with the result. The machine picked out the lines and architectural details of the building, making a personalised piece that would suit a keepsake or gift. It's the kind of project that shows why I'd pick a Maker over an Explore if you want to experiment with different materials and techniques.

In a recent development, I also used the Maker 5 to engrave and colour a set of toothbrush gifts (pictured) for someone in my village. The process was challenging but fun, and the Maker 5 powered through the set with ease.

In a recent development, the engraving tool works with the Maker 5, but it isn't included in every bundle, so check what you're buying. You can also buy it separately, and Cricut sells suitable metal and acrylic blanks. With the right tools, the machine can also deboss, score, and perforate, leaving plenty of room to experiment beyond straightforward cutting.

According to recent reports, personalised vinyl lettering is one of the easiest projects to start with. I've used Design Space to make name tags for items that need a little personalisation. Select Text from the menu, type the names, and choose your font and size. When you're happy with the design, load your Smart Permanent Vinyl with the coloured side facing up. The machine cuts around the letters, leaving you to remove the unwanted vinyl.

This is where patience and a micro-weeding tool come in handy. The tiny pieces inside letters such as 'e' and 'a' can be fiddly to pick out, particularly in smaller text. Next, cut a piece of transfer tape, peel off the backing, and place it over the design. Use a scraper to make sure the lettering sticks to the tape, then lift it away and press it onto your chosen surface. Permanent vinyl is already adhesive-backed, so you don't need any extra glue.

Recent findings suggest that iron-on vinyl works similarly, with two key differences. Switch on Mirror in Design Space before cutting, and place the iron-on with its shiny side down on the mat. That way, the lettering reads correctly when you transfer it to fabric with a heat press.

Print Then Cut is one of the most useful features if you like making colourful stickers, gift labels or personalised stationery. Instead of being limited to vinyl colours and effects, you print a full-colour design on your home printer and let the Cricut cut around the individual shapes.

Industry observers note that I use it for Christmas present labels. Create your design in Design Space, select Print Then Cut and send it to your printer. Once it's printed onto suitable printable vinyl or sticker paper, place the sheet on the Cricut mat and load it into the machine. The Maker 5 reads the registration marks and cuts around the printed designs, giving you colourful stickers with neat edges.

You'll need to buy printable vinyl or sticker paper separately, though, and the final results depend on your printer as well as the Cricut.

If you enjoy paper crafting, Design Space offers plenty to explore. You can choose pre-made templates, edit existing projects or start from scratch with your own images, shapes and text.

I've used it to make personalised Christmas gift tags, combining the machine's drawing and cutting functions. For one design, I set the machine to write a name with the pen, then switched to the fine-point blade to cut out the tag. For another, I used the blade to cut the lettering itself, which gives a different finish. Being able to write and cut in one project is useful, and Design Space makes it easy to arrange everything before you send the job to the machine.

You can also make paper flowers, boxes, cards, and Christmas decorations, with a huge range of templates you can customise in different colours, fonts, and materials. The included scoring tool helps here, giving you clean fold lines for cards and boxes.

Foil is another way to give cards, gift tags and decorations a more professional finish. The Maker 5 supports Cricut's Foil Transfer Tool, but you'll need to buy the tool and foil sheets separately.

Recent findings suggest that I used the Cricut Foil Transfer Kit, which costs around £43.49 and includes the tool, foil sheets and adhesive strips. It took me three attempts to get the result I wanted, but once I'd got the hang of it, the finish was excellent.

A few tips if you're trying it yourself:.

Once it's finished, unload the mat and carefully remove your card. The metallic detail makes handmade cards and gifts look far more polished.

You control the Maker 5 through Cricut Design Space, which is available on desktop and mobile. It's easy to install and walks you through each stage of a project. There's a huge library of ready-made designs, templates, and fonts, so you don't need to be confident with graphic design to get started; you can upload your own images or build designs from scratch.

Cricut has also added AI-assisted image generation, which is handy if you have an idea but don't have the illustration skills or software to create the artwork yourself.

In a recent development, the basic Design Space app is free, and you don't need a Cricut Access subscription to operate the machine. Access unlocks a much larger library of images, fonts, and ready-made projects, and some features and content depend on it, so it's worth factoring the ongoing cost into your budget if you expect to use the library regularly.

It has been revealed that what I like most is how the software guides you through the making process. Pick your project, choose your material, follow the instructions, and the machine does the hard work while you focus on the creative side.

Choosing a Cricut can be confusing with so many models around. The Maker 5 sits at the top of the range, but that doesn't mean it's right for everyone.

The Maker 4 is still very capable, and the two share much of the same cutting performance and tool compatibility.

The Maker 5 is smaller and lighter, has USB-C connectivity and a revised tool and pen-loading system, and handles compatible materials up to 3mm thick, compared with the Maker 4's 2.4mm.

In a recent development, both cut at up to 14.1 inches per second, so there's no speed advantage. If you already own a Maker 4, I'd only switch if the smaller footprint, lighter body or workflow improvements matter to you.

Sources indicate that the Explore 5 is much more affordable and ideal for everyday crafting. It handles vinyl, paper, cardstock and iron-on materials, and it's a great choice for stickers, cards, personalised gifts and decorations. It doesn't have the Maker's full range of tools, though.

If you're a quilter, want to cut fabric with a rotary blade, engrave metal, or work with more demanding materials, choose the Maker 5.

For many hobby crafters, the Explore 5 will be perfectly adequate. But if you want to grow into more ambitious projects, the Maker gives you far more flexibility.

Recent findings suggest that the Cricut Maker 5 is an excellent cutting machine, and versatility remains its biggest strength. Whether you're making personalised labels, Christmas decorations, paper flowers, cards, fabric patterns, or engraved keepsakes, it can do very little with the right tool and material.

I like how easy it is to set up and use. The smaller size is welcome; the lighter body makes it easier to move around, and the software takes much of the guesswork out of creating projects. Print Then Cut is great, and the engraving demonstrates how much potential there is beyond everyday vinyl and paper crafts.

Recent findings suggest that the extras add up, though. For quilting, you'll need a rotary blade and FabricGrip mat. Engraving, foiling and other specialist projects need their own tools and materials, and printable vinyl is another cost if you plan to make stickers. The supplied cardstock is useful for getting started, but I found it stuck to the mat when I tried to remove it, so peel it away carefully.

If you're upgrading from a Maker 3, the doubled cutting speed makes a compelling case. Maker 4 owners should be more cautious, as the smaller design and extra material thickness are useful, but the cutting performance is largely the same.

For anyone buying their first serious Cricut, though, the Maker 5 is a smart buy. It's easy to use, surprisingly compact for what it can do, and it lets you experiment with a huge range of projects. If you're a quilter or someone who likes to make a little bit of everything, this is the Cricut I'd choose.

Julie Dean is a former doctor and occupational therapist by profession, which inspired her to start sewing and quilting as a therapeutic activity. She is passionate about her craft and has been quilting and using Cricut for over five years. As well as selling her own designs and products on Etsy, Julie has taken commissions for interior design agencies to create bespoke quilts, including Beata Heuman. Julie's work has appeared in Architectural Digest.

Isern Serra designs bold colour-blocked interiors for Barcelona pilates studio

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.
  • Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.
  • “The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Salva López.

Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.

Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.

“The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.

“Although different in nature, both share a common philosophy centred on wellbeing, balance and the connection between body and mind,” he continued.

“Architecture plays an essential role in this experience, accompanying visitors on a gradual transition from the energy of the city towards a more intimate and introspective environment.”.

His studio introduced a series of colour-blocked spaces to guide customers through different phases of the interior, with colours that were specifically chosen to correspond to the function and tone of each area.

“This vision of wellbeing takes shape through a carefully choreographed sequence of spaces, where each change in level, colour and atmosphere guides consumers away from the bustle of the city and towards an increasingly introspective environment,” said Serra.

Serra combined cream banquette seating with dark wooden tables and alabaster sconces to create a calm, meditative environment for the cafe part of the space. A sculptural, mirrored service counter was also incorporated to reflect natural light around the space.

To signal the transition into the pilates studio, the designers introduced a deep-green reception hallway with tiered seating blocks and a spherical light installation.

The bright green circulation area is connected by an open archway and features curved architectural volumes that house the changing rooms, bathrooms and a water fountain.

Another rounded archway then leads to the main studio.

The main pilates studio was designed as a white space to reflect the coloured light from a sculptural LED light installation attached to the vaulted ceiling.

The aim was to create diverse exercise environments and enable the lighting to control the mood and energy of the space.

“The white surfaces act as a neutral canvas for coloured light, allowing different hues to transform the atmosphere,” Serra said.

“This system also offers flexibility for brand collaborations, as the lighting can be adapted to reflect different identities and experiences,” he added.

In the studio, the designers used mirrored walls to create the illusion of a circular room and added full-length perimeter curtains to soften the space’s texture.

Other interior projects recently featured on Dezeen include Matteo Thun designs for Milan’s Torre Velasca skyscraper and SABO’s design of an apartment on Manhattan’s Lower East Side.

Photography by Salva López.

#45496. Breaking: Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?
